segments.text: Welcome back! In this video and the next one, we're going to be talking about
materials and safety. Those go really hand in hand, so we'll talk some about
both throughout both videos. In this particular video, we're going to focus
mostly on materials. Materials are really important because we only allow
certain things to go into our laser to keep everyone safe. Laser cutting is
entirely safe if you do it correctly with the appropriate materials. If you
put the incorrect materials in the laser, there are risks of fire, there are risks
of unpleasant smells, of chemicals being released, all sorts of things we really
don't want to happen. And that is why we will give you this lovely laser
material list, which will list all of the requirements. We're going to also talk
through them in this video. The first and most important thing is every time
that you come in to use the laser, you will need to start by checking in with
staff at the lab info desk, and they will ask to check your materials to show
what you are using in the laser that day. You will need to both show them the
physical materials, so you'll need to show them your sheet of acrylic or
plywood or whatever you might be using. You will also need to show a label or
receipt or proof of purchase that says what that material is. What exactly
staff are looking for is a little bit different depending on your type of
material, and we'll cover all of that. But it's really important that you have
something that says, this is what I purchased. If you just show up with an
unlabeled piece of wood that you don't have a receipt or a label for, if you show
up with something that you found in your garage and you want to try
something on, we will turn you away and we will say that doesn't get to go in
our laser, because we're not certain what it is and we're not certain that it's
safe. Going down the list, you can start off with acrylic, and acrylic is nice and
simple because the only thing that we look for with acrylic is a label that
says the word acrylic. So that can be a label on the material, that can be a
receipt that says you bought a pack of acrylic from Hobby Lobby or Lowe's or
your web store of choice, that can be an email order confirmation that says I
purchased this off of Smokey Hills Designs or Inventables or the Extool
website. And as long as it says the word acrylic somewhere in that description,
you're good to go. Wood is slightly more complicated because we look for a couple
of more things. With wood we are looking at what type of wood it is because we
only allow hardwoods. Hardwoods have a little less sap, so they're a little
less flammable than softwoods which are going to have more sap within them and
not laser cut as nicely. So when you're looking at sheets of wood, we're going to
look for something that says basswood sheets like this. We're going to be
looking for something with a QR code, like this shows us that it was ordered
from Extool and does a label what the wood is. If you show up with just this
and you don't have an email or a physical receipt or something else that
tells us what this is, this will not be allowed to go in the laser. Even if it
is a laser safe material, if we don't have documentation, we're not going to
place it in the laser. With wood, we can also use high quality plywoods. So
those are going to be anything that's labeled as plywood. We don't want to
things like MDF board or sort of pseudo plywood or plywood with a lot of
other stuff mixed into it. When it comes to leather, the main thing that we are
looking for is that it is genuine vegetable tanned leather. Now when I say
genuine, that means it comes from a cow and we will be looking for something
that either says genuine leather, cowhide leather, real leather, anything that
specifies that this came from a cow and not imitation leather. We are also
going to double check that it says the words vegetable tanned and if it doesn't
specify, we will not allow it in the laser. So it's really important that it
specifies that because you will also find online things like chrome tanned
leather. Chrome tanned leather is not safe for lasers and if we're not certain
if it's chrome or vegetable tanned, we won't allow it in our laser. Along with
that, we will also not allow any sort of fake leather. So you might see things
like PU leather, laser bubble leather, imitation leather or pleather like it's
sometimes called and those can produce more fumes and we're not able to safely
do those here with the filtration system that we have. So we don't allow
any sort of fake or pseudo leather. It has to be cowhide or genuine leather.
You are not by any means limited to just cardboard sheets of wood. You can also
do things like this. So you can get larger pieces of acrylic. You can get
larger pieces of wood. You can find some that are pre-made. So you can find
cutting boards that are safe to laser. You can find utensils that are safe to
laser and anytime we do one of those, again, we just need some sort of label
or specification that says this is laser safe. This is the material it's made out of.
This shows that it's not been treated or stained or that there's other things we need to be worried
about. So if you just show up again with just this and it says this is a cutting board.
Doesn't get to go in the laser, but if you have something that says this is a cutting board that
is intended to be laserable, that is made out of walnut or cherry and is not currently stained or
treated, that we can allow. And you'll just want to be able to show us some sort of indication
that that's what that material is. You can also use paper, cardboard, and just general paper
products. So any sort of card stock, any sort of cardboard, those all work. And we're a lot
less concerned with those. The main thing we're going to be checking there is that they are free
from inks, stains, and adhesives. So we probably won't let you reuse your old Amazon box that's
still got all the glue stuck to it. But if you come in with a clean sheet of cardboard,
you are welcome to do that. If you come in with just some sheets of paper,
you're welcome to those. We don't need as much documentation that says, oh, this is
32 weight copy paper. We just need to be able to see that it's paper and doesn't have anything
currently on it. Like I said, at the start of this video, every time that you come in,
you will need to check in with staff at the lab info desk. And the staff have final say
on what does or does not go in the laser. So if you're ever unsure, if they're unsure,
they will almost always default to the cautious approach and not allow things in.
And we ask that you not argue with staff. Arguing with staff may result in suspension of your
ability to use the laser because staff have absolute final say on what does or does not go
into the laser here at the library. In the next video, we'll talk through some of the
physical safety features on the machine and what you need to know on that front.
